recall_prompt: Say the two definitions in your own words, and give one short example for the second one.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Define a set
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words "well-defined" and "distinct" are what the examiner reads for; a bare "a collection of objects" is not the definition.
lines: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects.
"Well-defined" means that for any given object it can be decided, without doubt, whether that object belongs to the collection or not.
The objects of a set are called its elements. If x is an element of A we write x ∈ A; if it is not, we write x ∉ A.
For example, {2, 4, 6, 8} is a set, but "the tall students of a class" is not, because "tall" fixes no clear test.

recall.must_convey: That a set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, with "well-defined" meaning membership can be decided for any object.

set ante well defined collection of distinct objects

steps.why: The two words "well-defined" and "distinct" carry the whole mark, because they are what separate a set from any other collection. A collection such as "the tall students of a class" fails the test, since membership cannot be decided.
common_mistakes: Writing only "a collection of objects" and leaving out "well-defined".
Listing a repeated object, as in {1, 1, 2}, which is the same set as {1, 2}.
Using ∈ between two sets, where ⊆ is meant.
steps.memory_tip: A collection is a set when the question "is this object in it?" has one clear answer for every object.

steps.label: Define the cardinality of a finite set
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give the symbol n(A) and one short example; a definition without the symbol reads incomplete.
lines: A set is finite when its elements can be counted and the counting comes to an end.
The number of distinct elements in a finite set A is called the cardinality, or the cardinal number, of A, and is written n(A).
For example, if A = {2, 4, 6, 8} then n(A) = 4, and n(∅) = 0.

lines.text: ∴ n(A) = the number of distinct elements of the finite set A.

recall.must_convey: That the cardinality of a finite set A is the number of distinct elements in it, written n(A).
accept: the cardinality is the number of distinct elements in the set

steps.why: Cardinality counts distinct elements only, which is why writing a member twice does not change n(A). It is a whole number, so the answer says how many elements there are, not which ones.
common_mistakes: Writing n(∅) = 1; the empty set has no elements, so n(∅) = 0.
Confusing n(A) with the number of subsets of A, which is 2 raised to the power n(A).
Giving the answer as a set, such as n(A) = {2, 4, 6, 8}, instead of a number.
steps.memory_tip: n(A) is a count, so the answer to a cardinality question is always a number and never a set.
